fframes: a halftone brick-toy data centre

How fframes makes video from Rust code, and how one silent 24-second film was built with it. Kept as a reference for next time.

Research note · fframes 1.4.2-rc.11 · written November 2026

1. What fframes is

fframes is a Rust library that renders video from code. A video is a Rust struct. For every frame the library calls render_frame(frame), and the method returns an SVG tree written with the svgr! macro. fframes draws that tree, then ffmpeg encodes the frames.

Rust struct implements Video→ render_frame per frame returns SVG→ Skia draws it (Metal GPU on a Mac)→ ffmpeg encodes MP4
PieceWhat it does
Video traitSets size, FPS, duration, audio, and render_frame.
Scene / ScenesSplits the timeline. Overlap::Previous(0.6) makes a cross-dissolve into the previous scene.
timeline!, frame.animateKeyframes and easing. Values are sampled per frame.
fframes::three_d (feature 3d)A three.js-style scene graph rendered with wgpu into an image, which the SVG then places with <image>.
ShaderRuns SkSL on the GPU over an image. Used here for the halftone.
Project CLItimeline, frame, strip, inspect, preview, render. Used to check the video without watching it.
The rule that shaped the work: all media logic stays in the Rust crate. No Python, shell or ffmpeg script cuts, retimes or grades anything. Python was used only to edit source text.

2. A very small example

The smallest useful video: one frame function, one animated value.

impl Video for Hello {
    const FPS: usize = 30; const WIDTH: usize = 1920; const HEIGHT: usize = 1080;
    fn duration(&self) -> Duration<'_> { Duration::Seconds(3.0) }
    fn audio(&self) -> AudioMap<'_> { AudioMap::none() }          // silent
    fn define_scenes(&self) -> Scenes<'_> { Scenes::from(vec![]) }

    fn render_frame<'a>(&'a self, frame: Frame, _ctx: &FFramesContext<'a, '_>) -> Svgr<'a> {
        // a circle that eases from x=300 to x=1600 over the first two seconds
        let x = frame.animate(timeline!(at 0.0 => 2.0, animate 300.0_f32 => 1600.0_f32, Easing::EaseInOut));
        fframes::svgr!(
            <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="1920" height="1080">
                <rect width="1920" height="1080" fill="#1d1f21" />
                <circle cx={x} cy="540" r="80" fill="#f2b81c" />
            </svg>
        )
    }
}

Check it without opening a player: frame 1s writes a PNG, strip all -n 8 writes a contact sheet, inspect --pops flags anything that jumps between two frames.

3. The example built here

The brief was a top-down, tilt-shift miniature of a busy data centre: technicians moving server racks, a glass office with two technicians and a developer, cool fluorescent light, status LEDs, cable trays, raised floor tiles and cooling units. Silent. It started photographic, and was later restyled as brick-toy figures under a halftone dot screen.

Structure

FileRole
src/lib.rsThe Video, three Shot scenes, camera framings, renderer settings, the halftone pass.
src/world.rsThe set (built once) and scene_at(t), which poses every person and moving object for time t.
src/people.rsThe brick-toy rig and the poses: walk, stand, push, seated, on the floor.
src/textures.rsProcedural textures: floor tiles, rack fronts, LED panels, carpet, cardboard.
src/shaders/halftone.skslThe dot screen.

One world, three camera moves

The 24-second action is a single continuous animation in world.rs. The three shots (Floor 0–8 s, Slot 7.4–15.5 s, Office 14.9–24 s) are only cameras over it, so people keep moving through the dissolves. A shot renders the world at world time = shot.start + frame.seconds().

fn render_shot(&self, shot: &Shot, frame: &Frame) -> Svgr {
    let t = shot.start + frame.seconds();
    let framing = shot.from.lerp(&shot.to, frame.animate(&shot.progress));
    let scene = self.world.scene_at(t);                       // pose everyone for time t
    let picture = self.renderer.render(&scene, &framing.camera(shot.blur));
    let image = self.halftone.draw(frame, ShaderUniforms::new()   // dot screen on the GPU
        .image("uSrc", &picture).float("uCell", 9.0).float("uBlock", 2.0));
    svgr!(<g opacity={opacity}><image href={image.href()} x="0" y="0" width={WIDTH} height={HEIGHT} /></g>)
}

The tilt-shift is real depth of field

No blur filter is painted on. The camera is a high oblique orbit (about 56–63° elevation, field of view 30) and focuses on a point, so the floor is sharp in a band and softens towards the top and bottom of the frame, exactly like a miniature photo.

Camera::perspective(30.0)
    .orbit(target, distance, azimuth, elevation)
    .focus_on(target + vec3(0.0, 0.8, 0.0), blur)   // focus at figure height, not on the floor
The blur strength was cut from 70–75 to 34 after adding the dot screen: strong blur under halftone turns the figures to mush. The focus point also moved up 0.8 m, because the heads sit above floor level and went soft.

People are rigs, posed per frame

scene_at(t) clones the static scene and writes joint angles for each figure. Paths come from Track, which builds KeyFramesAnimation segments between waypoints (EaseInOut) and bakes position, heading, speed and distance. The walk phase is taken from distance travelled, so feet do not slide.

// Tech A pushes the rack, walks round it, then pushes it north into the slot
let along = r1.dist / 0.55;
let pose = people::push(along, effort);
people::apply(&mut s, &rig, x, z, yaw, &pose);

Brick-toy figures

The figure is built from Geometry primitives: a lathe-turned cylinder head with a stud, a cap-shaped hair piece, an extruded trapezoid torso, block legs that swing from a hip axis, a rigid arm with a moulded bend, and a clip hand from a partial torus. Plastic comes from Material::standard(..).roughness(0.34).clearcoat(0.5). A toy has no knees, so walking is a stiff swing and the pelvis sinks as the legs spread, which keeps the feet on the floor.

The halftone shader

A GPU shader runs over each rendered 3D image. It does four things: it draws the picture in small pixel blocks, grades it (more saturation and contrast, a warm tone), samples the average tone of each 9-pixel cell, and draws one square dot per cell. The dot is dark on light surfaces and grows as the tone darkens. On near-black surfaces such as the racks it turns into a pale dot that grows with the light. Over strong colours the dot prints fainter, so the figures stay clean.

uniform shader uSrc;  uniform float uCell;  uniform float uBlock;

half4 main(float2 p) {
    half3 c = grade(uSrc.eval((floor(p / uBlock) + 0.5) * uBlock).rgb);   // pixel blocks
    float2 id = floor(p / uCell);
    float2 centre = (id + 0.5) * uCell;
    float lum = dot(cell_average(centre), half3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114));
    float d = max(abs(p - centre).x, abs(p - centre).y) * 0.8 + length(p - centre) * 0.2;
    float r = mix(r_pale, r_dark, smoothstep(0.13, 0.26, lum)) * mix(0.6, 1.2, hash(id));
    float dot_mask = 1.0 - smoothstep(r - 0.7, r + 0.7, d);
    return half4(mix(c, ink, half(dot_mask * strength)), 1.0);
}

Because the dots sit on a fixed screen grid (not on the 3D surfaces), they hold still while the camera moves and through the dissolves.

4. How it was checked

CommandUsed for
timelineConfirm scene ranges and the 720-frame length.
frame 11s,19sFull-size PNGs for lighting, colour and detail. --crop for zoomed checks.
strip Floor -n 8Judge motion and composition of each shot in one image.
inspect --popsFind one-frame jumps. It caught a technician snapping to a new heading at 14.0 s and a transparent wrap flickering at 0.2 s.
preview 0sReal-time window for a person to watch. Left for the user to open.

5. Lessons to reuse

  • The 3d feature needs the release candidate. It does not exist in fframes 1.4.0. Every fframes crate was pinned to =1.4.2-rc.11.
  • Build the world once, pose it per frame. Clone the static scene in scene_at(t) and write transforms. Instance repeated meshes (racks, trays) with Instances.
  • Make the camera the only difference between shots. People then carry across dissolves without any matching work.
  • Keep effects that fight each other in mind. Strong depth of field and a dot screen both destroy small detail. Tune them together.
  • Re-check after every pose change. inspect --pops and a crop around the interaction found collisions and snaps that a normal strip hid.
  • Transparent shells flicker. A clear wrap box next to transparent shadow decals changed draw order from frame to frame. Dropping the wrap fixed it.
  • Skia runtime shaders need constant loop bounds and no while. Sample the source with uSrc.eval(coord) in the image's own pixels.

6. Reproduce

cargo fframes new datacentre --format landscape --fps 30 --yes   # then enable features ["3d","wgpu"] and pin rc.11
cd datacentre
cargo build --release
./target/release/datacentre timeline
./target/release/datacentre frame 11s
./target/release/datacentre inspect --pops
cargo run --release -- preview 0s
cargo run --release -- render                                     # final export, only when wanted

Output: 1920×1080, 30 fps, 24 s, silent, libx264 CRF 20.
